newsitem.title: THAILAND: Gloom deepens in troubled Thai finance sector.
newsitem.headline: Gloom deepens in troubled Thai finance sector.

text.p: Gloom in the bruised Thai finance industry grew with new provisioning and capital hike burdens as finance firms struggled to cope with huge low quality assets and a bearish stock market, analysts said on Tuesday.

They said despite a government pledge to back cash-strapped finance companies facing possible runs on their deposits, the measures announced by the Bank of Thailand would likely lead to the biggest shakeout for the industry since the early 1980s.

"I don't see a shred of confidence in and outside Thailand now. Business and consumer confidence is not built overnight and it is a long-term proposition to regain it," said a foreign analyst, who declined to be named.

Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond instructed commercial banks and finance firms on Monday to raise provisions for sub-standard assets to 115 and 120 percent respectively from earlier 100 percent.

He said the increase, designed to boost the stability of Thai financial institutions, would require these companies to set aside an additional 50 billion baht ($1.94 billion) of reserves for low quality loans.
Of the increased provisions, 24 billion baht would be made by banks and the remaining 26 billion by finance companies within two years.
Thai banks and finance firms saw earnings plunge last year, largely due big loan exposures to an ailing Thai property sector which have faced a severe slump since 1993.

A foreign analyst estimated that about 8.8 percent of total outstanding loans of Thai banks and finance firms could be classified as sub-standard and doubtful. He said the quality of these assets would deteriorate fast and their size grow as the property slump continued.

The central bank governor said 10 finance firms with short-term cashflow problems were also ordered to hike capital by 8.25 billion baht immediately to boost confidence of their creditors that they could continue to operate soundly.
"It is a step in the right direction and it will boost the bank and finance sector in the long run," said Kavee Chukijkasem of Capital Nomura Securities Plc.
Analysts were unanimous that the required higher provisions would hurt earnings of about 90 Thai finance firms more than banks, which mostly already had sufficient provisions.
About 41 finance and securities firms are listed on the Stock Exchange of Thailand.
Kavee of Capital Nomura projected that earnings of the finance sector would contract a further 30 percent this year from a weak 1996 when overall profits declined about 15 percent.
Pipat Ronnakiart, chief analyst at Adkinson Securities Plc, said he expected battered Thai stocks to bear the negative impact of the central bank measures this week.
The Thai exchange's SET Index has retreated 48 percent in the past year.

Analysts said the central bank would use the new provision requirement to help realise its long standing policy of consolidating the finance sector by trimming the number of companies through merger and acquisition.

Governor Rerngchai said on Monday a fund run by the central bank would provide credits to help the 10 finance firms raise capital and the authorities would review the possibility of encouraging their future mergers.
